blocks.prompt: The Hospital That Comes to You
blocks.text: An ambulance is a little hospital room with wheels. Inside there is a bed, a tank of air, and a box of tools. Two helpers ride along. They are called paramedics. When you call for help, the ambulance comes to you. The lights flash blue and red. The siren wails so cars know to pull over. Look at the front of an ambulance. The word is written backward. That is not a mistake. When a driver sees it in the mirror, it flips around and reads the right way.

blocks.prompt: A Hospital That Drives
blocks.text: Most of the time, when you are sick, you go to the doctor. An ambulance flips that around. The hospital comes to you. The name gives away the idea. Ambulance comes from an old Latin word that means to walk. Long ago, armies built hospitals that could pack up and walk along behind the soldiers. The name stuck, even after the walking hospitals grew wheels and engines. An ambulance is really a small room built to move. Inside there is a stretcher that rolls, tanks of oxygen, bandages, and a machine that can shock a stopped heart back into rhythm. Two paramedics ride in the back. They do not just drive you to the help. They are the help. Treatment starts the moment they reach you. Look at the front of an ambulance and you will see the word printed backward. That is on purpose. A driver ahead of it sees the word in the mirror, which flips it, and reads it the right way around.

blocks.prompt: The Flying Ambulance
blocks.text: For most of history, being wounded in a battle meant waiting. The fighting had to stop first. Only then would carts roll out to gather up the injured, sometimes a full day later. By then, many of the people who could have been saved were long past saving. A French army surgeon named Dominique Jean Larrey watched this happen and decided it was absurd. In the 1790s he built something new: light, fast carriages set on springs, pulled by horses, staffed by trained crews who carried supplies with them. They did not wait for the battle to end. They drove into it. Larrey called them ambulances volantes, which means flying ambulances. Larrey added a second idea that was, at the time, close to shocking. When the wounded arrived, he treated the most badly hurt first. Not the officers first. Not his own countrymen first. The worst wounds first, no matter which army the man had been fighting for. He called this sorting triage, from a French word meaning to pick out. Nearly every emergency room on Earth still does it his way. Both ideas came from one insight. In an emergency, time is the enemy, and how you spend the first few minutes decides almost everything that follows. The vehicle parked outside a hospital today looks nothing like a horse cart on springs. It is doing exactly what Larrey's cart did.

notes: Boxy so a paramedic can stand up and work
Sirens slide and yelp because one flat note is hard to locate
The pitch drop as it passes is the Doppler effect
Yellow green registers fastest in daylight
The blue Star of Life has six points for six steps

blocks.prompt: Why an Ambulance Is Built Like a Room
blocks.text: An ambulance is not really a vehicle with medical gear stuffed inside it. It is a medical room that happens to have an engine bolted to the front, and almost every strange thing about it follows from that. Start with the shape. It is a box because a paramedic has to stand upright, reach all sides of a patient, and open a cabinet while the whole thing is cornering at speed. A car cannot offer that. Neither can a station wagon, which is what American ambulances mostly were until the 1970s, and which is why crews spent years working on their knees. Then the sound. A siren does not hold one note, and that is deliberate. A single steady tone is surprisingly hard to locate. Your brain figures out where a sound came from by comparing what each ear receives, and in a street full of walls that bounce sound in every direction, one clean note gives it very little to work with. A tone that slides, warbles and yelps keeps handing your ears fresh information. Something else happens to that siren as it goes past you. Coming toward you it sounds high. The instant it passes, it drops. The siren itself did not change at all. Each wave of sound left the ambulance from slightly closer than the one before it, so the waves bunched up and arrived more often, which your ear reports as a higher pitch. Once the ambulance is heading away, the waves stretch out and the pitch falls. This is the Doppler effect, and it is not a small piece of trivia. Astronomers aim the same idea at starlight and use the stretching of those waves to measure how fast distant galaxies are rushing away from us. Even the paint is an argument. That searing yellow green is not a style choice. In daylight, human eyes are more sensitive to yellow green than to any other color, so it registers before red does. The blue six pointed star on the side is called the Star of Life, and its points stand for the six steps of an emergency: someone notices, someone calls, help is sent, help arrives, care continues on the road, and the patient is handed over at the hospital. None of it is decoration. Every part of an ambulance is an answer to a question somebody asked after something went wrong.

notes: In 1965 the ambulance was often a funeral home hearse
A hearse was the only vehicle built to carry a person lying flat
Freedom House Ambulance Service, Pittsburgh, 1967
Trained by Dr. Peter Safar, the father of CPR
Crews recruited from the Hill District
Their training became the national paramedic standard

blocks.prompt: The Ambulance That Was a Hearse
blocks.text: If you were badly hurt in an American city in 1965 and somebody called for an ambulance, there was a fair chance the vehicle that pulled up was a hearse. This sounds like a joke. It was policy. A hearse was the only vehicle most towns owned that could carry a person lying flat, so funeral homes provided roughly half the ambulance service in the country. Much of the rest was handled by police, who loaded the injured into the back of a wagon and drove fast. Neither crew was trained to do anything else. Fast was the entire treatment plan. In 1966 a report from the National Academy of Sciences laid it out without mercy: a soldier shot in Vietnam had better odds of surviving than a person injured on an American highway, because the soldier was reached by medics who knew what they were doing. Pittsburgh's Hill District had it worse than most. The neighborhood was Black, and the police who answered its calls were slow when they came at all. People bled in their own doorways, waiting. In 1967 an unlikely partnership formed. Freedom House Enterprises, a community organization in the Hill District, joined forces with Dr. Peter Safar, an Austrian doctor at the University of Pittsburgh who had worked out how mouth to mouth breathing could be combined with chest compressions to restart a stopped heart. He is called the father of CPR. Safar wanted to prove a specific thing: that treatment should begin where the patient was lying, not thirty minutes later in a hospital corridor. To prove it he needed a crew willing to be trained properly, and nobody else was offering him one. The recruits came from the Hill District itself. Many were unemployed. Some had been written off by every employer who had ever looked at them. Safar put them through hundreds of hours of instruction, far past anything an ambulance crew in America had ever been asked to learn: airway management, CPR, defibrillation, intravenous lines, reading heart rhythms, delivering babies. They took the name Freedom House Ambulance Service, and they were the first paramedics in the United States in the sense we now use that word. They were extraordinarily good. They arrived, they assessed, they treated on the spot, and their patients survived at rates nobody else in the city could match. Doctors who had assumed the experiment would embarrass everyone rode along and came back convinced. The curriculum Safar built for them became the template for paramedic standards nationwide. The ambulance that shows up at your address today, staffed by people who start work in your driveway, exists because Freedom House proved it could work. In 1975 the city took over emergency services and closed Freedom House down. A few of the medics were hired into the new citywide service. Many were not. The men who had invented the job were told, in effect, that the job would carry on without them. That ending belongs in the story, and leaving it out would be dishonest. So does this. Every idea that mattered survived. Look inside a modern ambulance. The stretcher, the drug box, the heart monitor, the crew who kneel down and get to work before the wheels have finished turning. That is the Hill District's design, and it is still on the road.
